clue.text: Demonstrate outside home about Northern Ireland?

indicators.note: outside says the word for demonstrate goes round the remaining letters

explanation.surface: Protesting around the house about the situation in Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern Ireland is often simply called 'the Province' in Britain; the question mark marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Northern Ireland is a region of the UK commonly referred to as a province, Ulster being one of Ireland's four.

clue.text: Very good exercises for music-maker

explanation.surface: A musician is praised for their practice routine.
explanation.walkthrough: PI (short for pious) is a crossword staple for 'very good' or 'holy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe is a simple wind instrument, so it makes music.

clue.text: Writer after short time turning up on American vehicle

indicators.note: after places the writer's piece behind the short time
on in a down clue puts the first part above the next
in a down clue, turning up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a short time

explanation.surface: An author arriving after a brief delay on a US bus.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is the full old name for a bus, a public road vehicle.

clue.text: I can run riot, somehow creating insurmountable barrier

indicators.note: the letters come together in some unspecified order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that their rampage will throw up an impassable wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run riot' looks like the signal to rearrange, but those letters are fodder; the signal comes after the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical name: the Iron Curtain was the Cold War division of Europe, a barrier people could not cross.

clue.text: Yell having eaten that woman's fruit

indicators.note: the yell takes the pronoun inside itself, as if swallowing it

explanation.surface: Someone shouts because a woman's fruit has been eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the yell came because the fruit was eaten; in fact the yell does the eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain hypernym: the cherry is one kind of small stone fruit.

clue.text: Some mouse droppings — not fresh

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are taken

parts.note: the letters run from the third letter of mouse to the first of droppings

explanation.surface: Mouse droppings are found in the larder and they are not fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap: mo(USE D)roppings. 'Some' reads as a quantity of droppings, not an instruction to take part of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something used is second-hand, no longer fresh or new.

clue.text: Southern island's device for diver

parts.note: Cuba is a Caribbean island; the 's links it to the definition

explanation.surface: A southern island is known for gear used by divers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possession in the surface but works as 'is' in the cryptic reading: the island is the device.
explanation.definitionFit: Scuba is breathing apparatus that lets a diver stay underwater.

clue.text: Old comedian Ken before start of day was unsteady

parts.note: Ken Dodd, a long-serving British comedian

explanation.surface: An elderly comic tottered about before the day began.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Dodd was a British comedian famous for his wild hair and tickling stick, which is why 'Old comedian Ken' gives DODD.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodder is to move unsteadily, typically from age, so doddered means was unsteady.

clue.text: Gasp needing oxygen in family show?

indicators.note: the gasp needs the gas placed after it to finish the word

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: Someone gasping for air in the middle of a family show.
explanation.walkthrough: A panto (pantomime) is a British Christmas stage show for families, full of slapstick and audience shouting; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantomime is the classic British family entertainment at Christmas.

clue.text: Go into detail about former currency of UK

explanation.surface: Someone explains the history of Britain's old money.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'former currency' as one idea, like the shilling; split it and the prefix joins money that is still current.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound a subject is to explain it at length, going into detail about it.

clue.text: Favouring vivacity and speed, grow rapidly

explanation.surface: Someone who likes liveliness and pace urges fast growth.
explanation.walkthrough: A straight three-part build; the comma is only there for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cells or weeds that proliferate multiply fast, which is rapid growth.

clue.text: Salt transported to Caribbean

indicators.note: the letters are carried off and set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A cargo of salt is shipped to the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like a link word joining 'transported' to its destination, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bicarbonate is a salt of carbonic acid, as in sodium bicarbonate.

clue.text: Expert countryman protecting cold bird

indicators.note: the outer letters surround the cold letter, shielding it

parts.note: a dab hand is an expert

explanation.surface: A skilled farmer shelters a bird from the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert countryman' reads as one person; the expert and the countryman are separate pieces, with the cold letter protected between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The dabchick is another name for the little grebe, a small water bird.

clue.text: Claim benefit around middle of March

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the benefit word goes round the central letter

parts.note: an asset is something of benefit or value

indicators.note: the middle of a five-letter word is its third letter

parts.note: the word March, whose centre letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone applies for a welfare payment partway through the third month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle of' March gives R, and ASSET goes 'around' it. 'Claim' is a verb here, not the benefit claim the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert something is to state it firmly as true, which is to claim it.

clue.text: Have a meal around six? Wonderful!

indicators.note: around means surrounding here, so the meal word encloses the Roman numeral

parts.note: to dine is to have a meal

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted at the idea of dinner at about six o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around six' pretends to be a rough time for dinner; it is an instruction to put the numeral inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Divine is used as an exclamation of delight, meaning wonderful.

clue.text: Perhaps one or two, say, lodging in Bury

indicators.note: the abbreviation lodges inside the other word

explanation.surface: One or two lodgers are staying in Bury, a town in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury, capitalised, looks like the Lancashire town, but it is the verb. 'Perhaps' signals that one and two are examples.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one and two are whole numbers, that is integers.

clue.text: Broadcast terrible news about leaders of the revolution

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled news goes round the leading letters
terrible news is news in a bad way, so its letters are thrown into disorder
the leaders of words are their first letters

parts.note: the first letters of the and revolution

explanation.surface: Awful reports are spread concerning the men who led an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' makes SEWN from NEWS, and it goes 'about' TR, the 'leaders of' the revolution. 'Broadcast' is the past participle meaning scattered, like seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed that is broadcast is scattered over the ground, so it has been strewn.

clue.text: Limited space in awful camp — torment

indicators.note: the letters are in an awful state, jumbled

explanation.surface: Prisoners are cramped in a dreadful camp and suffer.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash splits the fodder in the surface, but both words are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: A compartment is a small separate section, a limited space.

clue.text: Dance in the morning stopping unruly mob

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so the morning letters fill the middle of the jumbled mob
an unruly mob is out of order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning

explanation.surface: A dance held early in the day halts a riotous crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stopping' is not halting here but plugging: the morning letters sit inside the rearranged crowd, the way a stopper fills a bottle's neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The mambo is a Latin American ballroom dance of Cuban origin.

clue.text: Biblical children understand God ultimately

definitions.note: SEED is a collective noun, matching the plural children.

indicators.note: take the final letter of God

explanation.surface: Children in the Bible come to understand God in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Biblical' is fair because seed for descendants, as in 'the seed of Abraham', is mainly the language of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, seed means offspring or descendants.

clue.text: Huge chaps crammed into tumbledown semi

indicators.note: crammed into means squeezed inside, so the chaps go within the jumbled house
a tumbledown building is falling apart, so the letters of semi are rearranged

explanation.surface: A crowd of fellows is squeezed into a dilapidated semi-detached house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tumbledown' turns SEMI into IMSE, and MEN is 'crammed into' it. A semi is a semi-detached house, one of a pair joined by a shared wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Immense means enormous or vast, so it is a straight synonym of huge.

clue.text: Perspective of one of Germanic people coming to Britain

definitions.meaning: a point of view on a subject

definitions.text: one of Germanic people coming to Britain
definitions.meaning: a member of the tribe that gave England its name

explanation.surface: A historian's viewpoint on the Germanic tribes who invaded Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Angles, with the Saxons, came to Britain in the fifth century; 'England' comes from their name.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a slant or viewpoint taken on a matter, and a member of the Angles, a Germanic tribe.

clue.text: Experience negative vote being reported

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: a no is a vote against

explanation.surface: A politician has experience of losing a vote, as the news reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Experience' looks like a noun, but it is the verb: to have known hardship is to have experienced it.
explanation.definitionFit: To know something, such as hardship, is to experience it.

clue.text: Caused to be loved over grabbing attention

indicators.note: the word for over takes hold of the attention word, holding it inside

parts.note: to give an ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: Someone won affection by making a grab for attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' pretends to be a preposition; it means finished, as in 'the game is over'.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear someone is to make them loved, so endeared means caused to be loved.
